summary: Specifies the HTTP-based protocol for SCIM, a standardized service for managing identities across multiple domains, such as between an enterprise and cloud providers. It defines how to create, read, search, update and delete identity resources.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the set of requests computers send to add, find, change or remove a person from a shared list over the web.

questions: how does scim use http to manage users
what is a scim bulk request
subtitle: The HTTP and JSON protocol for creating, finding, changing and deleting users and groups across organizations.

tldr.problem: Organizations that provision users into many cloud services need one predictable way to create, search, update and remove identities, instead of a different API per provider.
tldr.mechanism: SCIM maps identity operations onto ordinary HTTP: POST to create, GET to read and search with filters, PUT and PATCH to modify, DELETE to remove, plus a Bulk endpoint, JSON bodies with the application/scim+json media type, and discovery endpoints.
tldr.outcome: Clients can manage users and groups in any compliant service provider the same way. RFC 7644 has since been updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967.

today: RFC 7644 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2015. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967, so read those together with it. It is the protocol half of SCIM; the schema is in RFC 7643.

sections.title: What the SCIM Protocol Is
sections.content:
The SCIM protocol is an application-level, HTTP-based protocol for provisioning and managing identity data in cross-domain settings such as enterprise-to-cloud or inter-cloud. It supports creating, modifying, retrieving and discovering core resources such as Users and Groups, as well as custom resources. The resources and attributes themselves are defined in RFC 7643.

Requests and responses carry JSON in the HTTP body, identified by the media type application/scim+json. Resources list their schemas in a schemas attribute. Protocol messages, such as list responses, errors and patch requests, are JSON objects whose schemas value begins with urn:ietf:params:scim:api:, and these message schemas are not discoverable through the /Schemas endpoint.

Because SCIM spans organizations whose schemas can differ, document validation is not recommended. The service provider interprets each request against its own schema and returns what it actually stored, so a client SHOULD NOT expect to get back exactly what it sent. For example, read-only attributes in a PUT are simply ignored, and the client does not have to strip them first.

All paths are relative to a Base URI that MUST NOT contain a query string, for example one that begins with https and ends in a path like /scim/.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM is a way to talk to a list of people using normal web requests. The answers come back as tidy labeled lists, and the server tells you what it really saved, even if that is a little different from what you asked.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
SCIM defines no authentication scheme of its own. It relies on TLS and standard HTTP authentication. The RFC lists examples that could be used: TLS client authentication, HOBA, bearer tokens (RFC 6750) with a framework such as OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749), proof-of-possession tokens, cookies for JavaScript clients, and HTTP Basic. Basic authentication is discouraged because it rests on a single, relatively static secret, and the RFC says implementers SHOULD combine it with other factors.

A service provider SHALL advertise its supported HTTP authentication schemes with the WWW-Authenticate header. Whatever method is used, the provider MUST be able to map the authenticated client to an access control policy. For example, a subject might be allowed to read and update only its own User resource. The authorization model itself is out of scope.

Bearer tokens in the examples are illustrative; they do not mean tokens are preferred. In some deployments, anonymous requests such as user self-registration may be acceptable, which Section 7.6 handles with extra safeguards.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM does not invent its own lock. It uses the locks the web already has, and the server must always know who is knocking and what they are allowed to touch.

sections.title: Endpoints, Creating and Retrieving
sections.content:
Each resource type has an endpoint named by pluralizing the type: /Users and /Groups. Clients SHOULD discover endpoints from /ResourceTypes because pluralization can be ambiguous. Other defined endpoints are /Me, /ServiceProviderConfig, /Schemas, /Bulk and a .search path extension for POST queries. The HTTP methods are used as follows: GET retrieves, POST creates (or searches, or bulk modifies), PUT replaces and MUST NOT be used to create, PATCH makes partial updates, and DELETE removes.

To create a resource, a client POSTs to the endpoint. The server ignores readOnly attributes in the body, and on success returns 201 Created with a Location header and the stored representation, which includes meta.location. A duplicate such as an existing userName yields 409 with a scimType of uniqueness. Retrieving a known resource is a GET on /Users/{id}, returning 200.

Three further features round out the basics. The /Me alias stands for the resource of the authenticated subject, and a provider that does not support it SHOULD answer 501. The base URL MAY include a version segment such as /v2/Users; at the time of writing the identifier is v2. Resource versioning uses standard weak HTTP ETags, and a client MAY send If-Match on PUT and PATCH, or If-None-Match on a GET. Multi-tenancy is optional and the protocol defines no scheme for it, but it names three ways to indicate a tenant: a URL prefix, a sub-domain or an HTTP header.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of thing has its own mailbox, like one for Users and one for Groups. Dropping a request in the right box creates, finds, fixes or removes something, and the server answers with a receipt.

sections.title: Querying: Filters, Sorting and Paging
sections.content:
A query can target a single resource, a resource type endpoint or the server root, and returns a ListResponse with totalResults, Resources, startIndex and itemsPerPage. A query with no matches still returns 200 with totalResults of 0. A server that would return too many results rejects the request with 400 and a scimType of tooMany.

Filtering is optional. The filter parameter uses attribute operators eq, ne, co, sw, ew, pr, gt, ge, lt and le, combined with and, or and not and grouped with parentheses. Square brackets let you apply several tests to the same value of a multi-valued attribute. Order of operations is grouping first, then logical operators (not, then and, then or), then attribute operators. An unrecognized operator makes the provider decline with 400 and invalidFilter.

Sorting (also optional) uses sortBy and sortOrder, which defaults to ascending. Pagination uses a 1-based startIndex (default 1) and count. Paging is not stateful, so clients MUST be prepared for inconsistent results between requests. The attributes and excludedAttributes parameters, which are mutually exclusive, trim which attributes come back. Clients can also POST a SearchRequest to a path ending in /.search, which keeps filter values out of the URL.
sections.plainLanguage: Searching is like asking the librarian for every book by one author, sorted by title, ten at a time. You say what you want, how to line them up, and which page to show.

sections.title: Replacing, Patching and Deleting
sections.content:
Implementers MUST support PUT, which replaces a resource's attributes. The server applies the mutability rules attribute by attribute: readWrite and writeOnly values replace existing ones, immutable values must match what is already set (otherwise HTTP 400 with scimType mutability is returned), and readOnly values are ignored. A required attribute MUST be given. Success returns 200 OK with the whole resource.

PATCH is optional (servers SHOULD support it since Groups may be large) and is modeled on JSON Patch (RFC 6902). The body has the schema urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp and an Operations array. Each operation has an op of add, remove or replace, an optional path and usually a value. Unlike JSON Patch, SCIM does not support array indexing or operations like move. A remove without a path fails with noTarget, and a replace whose filter matches nothing also fails with noTarget.

DELETE returns 204 No Content on success. A provider may keep the data but MUST return 404 for later operations on the resource and omit it from queries, and a deleted resource SHOULD NOT cause a later conflict on userName.
sections.plainLanguage: Replacing is handing in a whole new page. Patching is using a tiny eraser and pencil to fix just one line. Deleting is taking the page out, after which asking for it gets you a polite no such page.

sections.title: Bulk Operations
sections.content:
Bulk is an optional feature that lets a client send many operations in a single POST to /Bulk. The request uses urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:BulkRequest and an Operations array. Each entry has a method (POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE), a path, and for creating or changing, data. The response uses the BulkResponse schema and reports a status and location for each operation.

A client that creates something and needs to refer to it in a later operation gives it a temporary bulkId, which the server echoes back so the client can map it to the real id. This allows, for example, creating a User and adding that User to a Group in one request. The server MAY reorder operations for performance only if the result is the same as in-order processing, and MUST try to resolve circular references, though it MAY stop and return 409.

By default the provider continues past failures. The client can set failOnErrors to say how many errors to tolerate before the rest are abandoned. A provider MUST define a maximum number of operations and a maximum payload size, and an oversized request gets 413 Payload Too Large.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending a hundred little notes, you send one big envelope with all of them inside. You can give new things nicknames inside the envelope so later notes can point to them before they have real names.

sections.title: Errors and Status Codes
sections.content:
SCIM uses the HTTP status codes from the HTTP semantics specification, and errors MUST also be returned in a JSON body using the schema urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:Error. That body has a status string, an optional scimType keyword and an optional human-readable detail.

For HTTP 400 responses, the RFC defines these detail keywords: invalidFilter, tooMany, uniqueness, mutability, invalidSyntax, invalidPath, noTarget, invalidValue, invalidVers and sensitive. Other codes with SCIM-specific guidance include 401 and 403 for authorization problems, 404 for a missing resource or endpoint, 409 for version conflicts or duplicates, 412 when a resource changed on the server, 413 for oversized bulk requests, and 501 for unsupported operations such as PATCH.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the server does not just say no. It tells you which kind of mistake it was, like a bad search or a name that is already taken, so you can fix it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SCIM resources contain sensitive information, including passwords, so clients and providers MUST use transport-layer security. A service provider MUST support TLS 1.2 and clients MUST check the server's identity. Bearer tokens and cookies MUST carry enough entropy to resist guessing, MUST travel over TLS, and tokens MUST have a limited lifetime. A cookie SHOULD last no longer than a browser session.

Putting personal data in query filters on a GET risks leaking it into browser history and server logs. In such cases clients SHOULD query with POST (the .search form), and a server that receives sensitive filters in a GET SHOULD respond with 403 and the scimType sensitive.

For anonymous creation requests, the countermeasures include authenticating the web component that issues them, rate limiting, and creating new Users with active set to false until a secondary confirmation such as an email is completed. Stored credentials must not be in cleartext, and string comparisons for filters and uniqueness MUST use properly prepared Unicode strings.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything private has to travel in a sealed, locked bag. Do not shout secrets in the web address, where anyone walking by could read them. Be careful with strangers asking to sign up.

data.title: Filter examples
data.code:
filter=userName eq "bjensen"
filter=title pr and userType eq "Employee"
filter=meta.lastModified gt "2011-05-13T04:42:34Z"
filter=userType eq "Employee" and emails[type eq "work" and
  value co "@example.com"]

items.label: add
items.desc: Adds a value to an existing resource; replaces a single-valued attribute that already has one.

items.label: remove
items.desc: Removes the value at the required path; no path fails with noTarget.

items.label: replace
items.desc: Replaces the value at the path; a missing attribute is treated as an add.

items.label: Invalid filter
items.desc: The filter syntax was invalid or the attribute and comparison combination is unsupported.

items.label: Too many
items.desc: The filter yields more results than the server will process.

items.label: Uniqueness
items.desc: A value is already in use or reserved.

items.label: Mutability
items.desc: The change conflicts with the attribute's mutability or state.

items.label: Invalid syntax
items.desc: The request body did not conform to the request schema.

items.label: Invalid path
items.desc: The path attribute was invalid or malformed.

items.label: No target
items.desc: The path did not yield an attribute or value to operate on.

items.label: Invalid value
items.desc: A required value was missing or incompatible.

items.label: Invalid version
items.desc: The specified protocol version is not supported.

items.label: Sensitive
items.desc: Sensitive information was passed in the request URI.
